title: Etherscan Hacked? Crypto Users Have Had Enough as Support Security Scare Sparks Alarm
description:
Etherscan hacked? Freshworks, Optimizely, and major banking security incidents raise questions about crypto and traditional finance security.
The post Etherscan Hacked? Crypto Users Have Had Enough as Support Security Scare Sparks Alarm appeared first on Cryptonews.
fullContent:
Another day, another security scare. This time, Etherscan is warning users after detecting unauthorized access attempts against its customer support system that might have been hacked. But the timing could hardly be worse for an industry already dealing with a growing list of cyberattacks.

The warning comes just days after hackers exploited a vulnerability in Optimizely, injecting malicious code into websites operated by 178 organizations. The affected names included HSBC, BBC, Ledger, IKEA, Salesforce, Zoom, and CNN.

Meanwhile, crypto platforms have faced separate attacks involving compromised API keys, protocol vulnerabilities, and stolen customer information. Traditional banking has not escaped either, with a French bank recently losing approximately €100 million to hackers.

So what kind of security era are we entering? The problem is no longer confined to crypto exchanges or experimental DeFi protocols. Banks, technology companies, payment providers and blockchain businesses are increasingly exposed to the same interconnected digital infrastructure.

Discover: The Best Token Presales

Etherscan, Optimizely and 178 Websites Hacked: Nobody Seems Safe

Etherscan disclosed just a few minutes ago that attackers had attempted to gain unauthorized access to its Freshworks customer support and ticketing system. The company is investigating and has introduced precautionary measures. It has not confirmed that customer records were successfully accessed, but warned users about suspicious support communications, unexpected links, and requests for sensitive information.

The concern is particularly relevant because support impersonation remains an effective way to steal crypto and your money. An attacker posing as an Etherscan representative could exploit a user’s existing support request to make a phishing message appear legitimate.

But Etherscan is hardly the only name facing security questions this week. Just two days ago, hackers exploited a vulnerability in Optimizely’s Web Experimentation signup process. They injected malicious JavaScript into customer projects, allowing the code to run on websites using the affected software.

Security researchers identified 178 organizations whose websites carried the malicious code. The list included HSBC, BBC, Ledger, Zoom, Salesforce, CNN and Equifax. The injected script attempted to replace crypto wallet addresses with attacker-controlled alternatives. It also targeted payment-card information, cookies and screenshots, while attempting to deliver exploit code against older iPhones.

Optimizely confirmed the vulnerability and said it had removed the injected code and fixed the flaw. Its November 17 incident report said the unauthorized party exploited the signup process rather than stealing customer administrator passwords.

The financial damage remains unclear. It is reported that investigators could not establish how many visitors were affected or whether the attempted thefts succeeded.

The uncomfortable takeaway is that attackers did not need to breach 178 separate companies. They exploited one software provider whose code was embedded across hundreds of websites.

Crypto Exchanges and Banks Are Both Taking Hits

Crypto’s security problems extend beyond Etherscan and the Optimizely incident. DeFiLlama’s hack tracker recorded several attacks during the week, including a $10.39 million incident involving Lighter Perps on November 16. The attacker exploited a compromised trader API key, enabling unauthorized withdrawals.

Lighter said its protocol and smart contracts were not compromised. It temporarily suspended withdrawals and activated Guardian mode to prevent further unauthorized activity.

Another incident hit MORE Markets, where an attacker exploited a lending mechanism to drain approximately $308,000 in WFLOW. B18 TimeBank also suffered an exploit on November 17, losing $404,540 in USDC through its reward voucher redemption mechanism.

These incidents show different weaknesses across crypto infrastructure. Not every loss comes from a broken smart contract. Compromised credentials, vulnerable applications and flawed authorization mechanisms can be equally damaging.

Traditional finance faces its own problems. French lender Crédit Mutuel Arkéa disclosed a cyber heist earlier in November, with hackers stealing approximately €100 million through fraudulent transactions originating from the bank’s own accounts. The bank said customer assets were not affected, although some transactions were temporarily suspended.

Deutsche Bank also made headlines on November 17 after confidential internal documents surfaced through an international journalistic investigation. It was a document leak, not a confirmed breach of its current banking systems.

Deutsche Bank said security testing found no indication that its current IT environment, account information, login credentials, or payment data had been compromised. Yet, it has greater effects to geopolitics.

Banking institutions are not immune to major security incidents simply because they operate under traditional financial regulations.

Is Crypto Actually Less Safe Than Traditional Banking?

Crypto has suffered enormous losses. The October Binance incident alone involved $6.3 billion in stolen digital assets, making it one of the largest cryptocurrency heists on record. Yet, traditional finance also faces attacks involving payment infrastructure, third-party service providers, and internal transaction systems.

The Optimizely incident is particularly revealing. Both HSBC and Ledger appeared among the affected organizations. The vulnerability did not care whether visitors were interacting with a traditional financial institution or a crypto company.

Neither system offers complete protection. The real question is whether companies can secure the increasingly complex infrastructure connecting their services. A single compromised vendor can expose hundreds of organizations, while one stolen credential can bypass otherwise sophisticated security systems.

Crypto users have every reason to demand stronger protections. But traditional banking customers should not mistake regulation and familiar branding for immunity.

With Etherscan possibly being hacked, the data provider is now joining the growing list of companies investigating security incidents.

title: Cognizant and Qualys Redefine AI-Era Managed Security Service
description: Cognizant will use the full Qualys portfolio to bring its clients what the frontier AI era demands: AI-speed detection, hyper-prioritization, and confident remediation for every zero-day. When a critical zero-day goes public, security leaders ask two questions: which assets are affected, and how fast can we safely fix them? For most enterprises, the current answer […]
fullContent:
Cognizant will use the full Qualys portfolio to bring its clients what the frontier AI era demands: AI-speed detection, hyper-prioritization, and confident remediation for every zero-day.

When a critical zero-day goes public, security leaders ask two questions: which assets are affected, and how fast can we safely fix them? For most enterprises, the current answer is days, then weeks.

Frontier AI makes that remediation timeframe dangerous. Microsoft’s November Patch Tuesday alone carried 1,093 vulnerabilities, up from 93 in November 2025 before frontier AI models arrived. AI-assisted attackers can weaponize a new advisory in four to twelve hours, while scan-driven detection often takes 24 to 36 hours just to show which assets are affected. The risk is already real: Cognizant’s 2026 Cybersecurity Pulse Poll found that 83% of participating U.S. enterprises had an AI-related security incident in the past 24 months.

Knowing what to fix is only half the gap. Every step from finding to fix is still gated by people, for one reason: fear that a patch will break production, that a reboot will take down a critical system, or that there is no fast way back. Teams will not hand fixes to automation they do not trust.

Cognizant helps the world’s largest enterprises scale with AI, through its AI Builder approach, and recognizes that its clients need security that moves at machine speed. Already running managed services on Qualys ETM, Cognizant is now expanding to the full Qualys portfolio, including TruRisk Eliminate. That is why I am excited to welcome Cognizant to the Qualys Global mROC Alliance.

Managed detection is table stakes. This is the dawn of the 24-hour autonomous remediation service, run from Qualys ETM: a zero-day disclosed, detected, prioritized, and remediated within a day.

Why the Qualys Platform Fits Cognizant’s Approach

Running zero-day response as a service, at enterprise scale, puts specific demands on the platform underneath. Cognizant needed three capabilities working as one:

  • One record for every asset, across every tool, built from Qualys and non-Qualys sources, so there is no reconciling data across disparate tools before anyone can act.
  • Exploit validation in each client’s own environment, so every hour of the client’s team’s time goes to risk that is real.
  • Remediation with confidence, so automation can be trusted within production systems.

Qualys delivers all three on one platform, with the agentic AI to run them at machine speed.

Cognizant brings what a platform alone cannot: Cyber Vulnerability Management services and threat intelligence, delivery experience inside large enterprises, and a view of risk in financial terms for the board. Its operators run the Risk Operations Center, powered by Qualys ETM to navigate inside each client’s own tools, change windows, and approvals. Clients keep control of what gets fixed and when. Cognizant carries the daily work.

“Our 2026 Cybersecurity Pulse Poll shows that strength in one control, such as detection or remediation, still leaves enterprises exposed in the AI era. Together with Qualys, we are connecting detection, prioritization and remediation into one managed operating model, helping clients reduce risk, strengthen resilience and scale AI with confidence.”
— Vishal Salvi, SVP and Global Head of Cybersecurity, Cognizant

Cognizant will deliver four mROC services on the Qualys platform:

  • Cyber risk quantification and advisory services. Cyber risk for business applications shown in dollars, with a personalized risk plan and a report for the board.
  • Onboarding and integration. The security tools a customer already owns connected into one record for each asset, with data quality checked from day one.
  • Risk monitoring as a managed service. AI-speed alerts on new CVEs, a validated queue instead of noise, and a weekly exposure review, using InstaScan, Agent Val, and ROCky.

Risk remediation as a managed service. A wave-based plan built from the Risk Elimination Playbook, zero-touch remediation where it is safe, and proof the fix held, using TruRisk Eliminate, TruConfidence, and Agent Sara.

AI-Speed Detection: Every Exposure Known in Minutes

Frontier AI has changed the rhythm of disclosure. Vulnerabilities now land in volume, and attackers act on them in hours, well inside any scan cycle.

Qualys InstaScan, delivered by Agent Insta, closes that gap. It turns the inventory and telemetry a client already has, from Qualys and non-Qualys sources, into high-confidence findings within minutes of disclosure. No new scan, no new agent.

On November’s Patch Tuesday, InstaScan delivered 90% of detections within minutes. The first landed about 40 minutes before Microsoft’s own release notes went live. With Cognizant, that speed turns into action. Through its risk monitoring service, Cognizant analysts watch for new disclosures every day, confirm each exposure, and route it to the right asset owner with context. The client’s team no longer chases owners or rebuilds asset lists every time a new CVE trends.

Hyper-Prioritization: Proven Exploitability

More vulnerabilities do not mean more risk. Of the 48,172 vulnerabilities disclosed in 2025, the Qualys Threat Research Unit found only 357 (0.74%) confirmed remotely exploitable and actively weaponized. No team can work the full list, and none should have to.

Agent Val and TruConfirm test what is actually exploitable in the client’s own environment, with existing controls counted. Critical on paper but blocked by a control? It leaves the urgent queue. Exploitable on a PCI-scoped server? It goes to the top.

Cyber Risk Quantification (CRQ) then puts validated risk in dollars, by business application, so the CISO can show the board what each fix is worth.

With Cognizant, the short list becomes a working rhythm. Through its risk monitoring and advisory services, Cognizant keeps each client’s validated queue current and reviews it with them every week. The client’s team stops triaging noise and starts each week knowing exactly what to fix first.

Autonomous Remediation: Remediate with Confidence and Maintain Operational Resiliency

That fear is why the global mean time to remediate sits at about 30 days. TruRisk Eliminate, with TruConfidence, removes it by protecting operational resiliency before, during, and after every change.

  • Before: TruRisk Eliminate chooses the safest fix for each finding: patch, mitigate, isolate, or uninstall. A patch reliability score decides what deploys automatically and what goes ring by ring.
  • During: Changes roll out in waves, starting with low-risk rings. System health is watched through each wave, and rollback restores a known-good state if health drops.
  • After: AI-powered patch failure analysis pinpoints why a change failed and the corrective actions, and automated rollback restores a known-good state.

Showing clients the 1% that matters

Cognizant can open every client engagement with a Risk Elimination Playbook, powered by TruConfidence and built for that client’s environment. It narrows the backlog to the 1% that must be fixed now and moves the rest into planned software updates. It also benchmarks the client’s mean time to remediate against peers, and shows how much of the backlog autonomous remediation can close, and how much faster.

It becomes the plan behind every remediation wave and the baseline for every review.

Where Managed Security Goes Next

The three pillars together provide a new kind of service: 24-hour autonomous remediation, run from ETM. Cognizant can take a critical zero-day from disclosure to remediation within a day, for every client, with operational resiliency built in at every step.

Managed security is moving from raising alerts to closing risk. Cognizant is among the first to deliver that at enterprise scale, and I expect it to set the bar enterprises hold every provider to. That is what the Global mROC Alliance was built for: the platform, the certification path, and the operating model to run the Risk Operations Center as a service.

Attackers already move at AI speed. This expanded partnership helps tip the balance back toward the defense.

title: Arbitrum Price Drops 19% in Seven Days Despite $7.4M Revenue and USDG Growth
description: Arbitrum booked $7.4 million in revenue and USDG lending passed $153 million, yet ARB fell 19% in a week. Buyers now need to defend support near $0.11.
fullContent:
Arbitrum's latest revenue report shows a network earning steady income from several sources, with stablecoin demand climbing alongside it.

ARB holders have little to show for it. The token kept sliding with a weak crypto market this week. Traders now want to know whether stronger fundamentals can ever lift a token that earns no direct share of fees.

Arbitrum Books $7.4M as USDG Lending Passes $153M

Arbitrum reported $7.4 million in recent revenue in a post on the network's official X account. The haul lifts its 2026 total above $13.6 million. For a layer 2 network that sells faster and cheaper Ethereum transactions, that is a meaningful income line.

The money comes from five separate streams. Transaction fees make up one source, and treasury management makes up another. Spreading income across several channels means the network leans less on any single business.

Stablecoin activity is also growing. Adoption of USDG, a dollar-pegged token, keeps rising on Arbitrum. Lending of USDG on Morpho, a decentralized lending protocol, now holds more than $153 million in total value locked. That figure measures the deposits users have committed to the market, and it signals growing trust in the asset.

Arbitrum has also built ties with traditional finance. The network counts Cross River Bank and SBI Digital Markets as partners. Both firms give the ecosystem a bridge to regulated banking and capital markets, which could draw more institutional users over time.

A Broad Crypto Selloff Swallows the Good News

Those revenue numbers arrived at an awkward moment. Crypto markets are in a broad retreat, and bitcoin is leading the way down. Bitcoin has dropped about 13% over the past week, dragging most major tokens with it.

ARB has fared worse. The token fell roughly 19% over the same seven days. That gap is common for layer 2 tokens, which tend to swing harder than bitcoin in both directions. When traders cut risk, smaller and more speculative assets usually get sold first.

The network's design also limits the boost from good news. Arbitrum's income flows to its DAO treasury, the pool of funds governed by token holders. ARB holders receive no direct share of those fees.

Treasury Gains While Token Holders Wait

The split between network income and token price creates clear winners and losers.

  • DAO and treasury: Steady revenue pays for operations and funds grants without forcing large token sales.
  • ARB holders: The token has lost about 31% over the past month. For now, those price losses outweigh any comfort from stronger fundamentals.
  • USDG issuers and Morpho lenders: Rising stablecoin demand brings more deposits, more borrowing and more fee income.
  • Rival layer 2 networks: Competitors face pressure to show income of their own, or risk looking weaker to builders and investors.

$0.11 Becomes the Floor Bulls Cannot Lose

Arbitrum (ARB) daily price with the nearest support (green) and resistance (red). Source: TradingView

ARB trades near $0.13, down about 3% in the past day. The token sits below its 50-day average near $0.16. It also trades under its 200-day average. Both lines now act as ceilings, which keeps the broader trend in sellers' favor.

Momentum is weak as well. RSI, a 0 to 100 gauge of momentum, reads 35. That is weak but short of oversold, so there is still room for further selling before buyers typically step in. The MACD indicator also points down.

On the daily chart, the green line marks support near $0.11. Holding that level is the main job for buyers. A clean break would expose the next support around $0.083, a much deeper drop.

Any rebound faces the red line near $0.15. That level matches the 200-day average, which makes it a tough barrier to clear.

What Could Turn ARB Around Next

Three things could shift the picture for ARB in the coming weeks.

  • Revenue and USDG growth: Another strong income update, plus rising USDG deposits on Morpho, would show the network keeps gaining users.
  • Bitcoin's direction: If bitcoin steadies, selling pressure on altcoins like ARB could ease.
  • A close above $0.17: A daily close past that level would signal buyers have returned with real conviction.

title: Medicare's 2027 price hikes will take a bite out of retirees' Social Security checks
description:
Medicare Part B premiums will rise by 3.2% in 2027, the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services announced Tuesday.
The standard premium will rise by $6.50 per month to $209.40, totaling a $78-per-year increase. 
The 2027 increase, far smaller than the nearly 10% increase enrollees faced in 2026, is in line with the 3.25% increase projected by Medicare's trustees.
According to the CMS, "The increase in the 2027 Part B standard premium and deductible is mainly due to projected increases in healthcare spending."
Here's what you need to know before the increases are applied in January.
What else is changing?
The Medicare Part A deductible, which beneficiaries pay if they are admitted to the hospital, will rise by $40 to $1,776 in 2027.
The Medicare Part A premium will be $597 per month, a $32 increase from $565 in 2026. 
According to the CMS, it is paid by:

Anyone aged 65 and older with fewer than 40 quarters of coverage, plus certain people with disabilities.

Uninsured people aged 65 and older with fewer than 30 quarters, and certain people with disabilities who have exhausted other entitlements.

Those with at least 30 quarters (or a spouse with 30 or more quarters) will pay a reduced rate of $328. 



Roughly 9% of people with Part B pay an income-related surcharge on top of their monthly premium.
The annual deductible for all Medicare Part B beneficiaries will increase by $9 to $292 in 2027.
In 2027, individuals with modified adjusted gross income above $112,000, or couples filing jointly above $224,000, will pay more. At the top tier, individuals with an income of $500,000 or more and couples earning $750,000 or more will pay $711.80 a month.



Married people who live with their spouse but file separate tax returns pay the standard $209.40 Part B premium if their income is $112,000 or less. Above that, they pay a total of $670 a month, rising to $711.80 for those earning $388,000 or more.
A small group of kidney transplant patients can keep Part B coverage of immunosuppressive drugs for a standard premium of $125.70 a month.
Those with higher incomes who pay Part D premiums face separate income-related surcharges between $15.40 and $96.40 a month on top of their plan's premium. The surcharge is paid to Medicare and is either deducted from Social Security checks or paid directly.
How will this affect Social Security payments?
People who have their Part B premium deducted from their Social Security checks will keep less of the cost-of-living adjustment next year.
For the average retiree, the $6.50 Part B increase will eat into the $75 monthly COLA boost, leaving them with about $68.50 more a month.
Most beneficiaries will have the standard $209.40 Part B premium withheld from their checks. Higher earners will pay more, with total monthly Part B premiums reaching as much as $711.80 and Part D surcharges up to $96.40.

title: Cathie Wood’s ARK Sells $85 Million In Nvidia While Buying $40 Million In Crypto Stocks — What’s Behind The Shift?
description: Cathie Wood’s ARK Invest has made a striking portfolio adjustment, selling approximately $84.8 million in Nvidia shares while purchasing nearly $40 million in cryptocurrency-related stocks. The transactions come as Bitcoin ETFs face renewed market pressure, raising an important question: are institutional investors beginning to identify opportunities in crypto-related businesses despite the broader market downturn? According […]
fullContent:
Cathie Wood’s ARK Invest has made a striking portfolio adjustment, selling approximately $84.8 million in Nvidia shares while purchasing nearly $40 million in cryptocurrency-related stocks. The transactions come as Bitcoin ETFs face renewed market pressure, raising an important question: are institutional investors beginning to identify opportunities in crypto-related businesses despite the broader market downturn?

According to ARK’s November 16 trading disclosures, the investment firm sold 543,092 Nvidia shares across its ARK Innovation ETF (ARKK) and ARK Next Generation Internet ETF (ARKW).

Using Nvidia’s closing share price of $156.14, the transaction was valued at approximately $84.8 million. The actual proceeds could differ because the trade disclosures report share quantities rather than execution prices.

Meanwhile, ARK increased its exposure to several companies operating within the cryptocurrency and digital payments industries.

Cathie Wood’s ARK Makes A $40 Million Crypto Stock Bet

ARK’s purchases included 277,523 shares of Block, the financial technology company associated with Jack Dorsey and Bitcoin-focused payment products.

Those shares represented an estimated $23 million investment, making Block the largest crypto-related equity purchase disclosed for the session.

The firm also acquired 180,534 shares of stablecoin issuer Circle, worth approximately $10.4 million, alongside 53,760 shares of Coinbase, valued at around $6.4 million.

Combined, the purchases totaled approximately $39.9 million.

Interestingly, all three companies experienced share-price declines during the trading session. Block fell 1.92%, Circle declined 7.29%, and Coinbase dropped 6.11%.

Rather than waiting for prices to recover, ARK increased selected positions while market sentiment remained weak.

However, these transactions involved publicly traded companies, not direct purchases of Bitcoin or other cryptocurrencies.

Why Did ARK Sell Nvidia While Buying Crypto Companies?

The timing is particularly interesting because Nvidia has become one of the most recognizable companies associated with artificial intelligence infrastructure.

ARK’s decision to reduce its Nvidia exposure while increasing selected cryptocurrency-related positions may suggest an effort to rebalance exposure across different technology sectors.

However, interpreting the move as a complete departure from artificial intelligence would be misleading.

ARK had purchased additional Nvidia shares earlier in November and continued to maintain a substantial position after the latest sale.

The investment manager also acquired approximately $52 million worth of SpaceX shares during the same trading session.

Furthermore, ARK reduced its holdings in Bullish and sold units of Ethereum and Solana staking exchange-traded funds.

These transactions suggest a more selective investment approach rather than an unrestricted shift into cryptocurrency assets.

ARK’s own research provides another perspective. In its November 17 newsletter, the firm described Block as an AI company, highlighting the increasingly blurred boundaries between financial technology and artificial intelligence.

What Could This Mean For Bitcoin And Institutional Adoption?

Although ARK’s purchases do not represent direct Bitcoin demand, they demonstrate continued institutional interest in businesses connected to digital assets.

Block’s involvement in Bitcoin payments, Circle’s stablecoin infrastructure, and the expansion of regulated cryptocurrency investment products all contribute to the broader digital asset economy.

This comes as BlackRock’s Bitcoin ETF activity continues to attract attention from institutional investors.

The distinction between investing in cryptocurrency directly and purchasing shares in companies supporting the industry remains important.

A crypto-related stock may respond to company earnings, regulation, equity-market conditions, and investor sentiment differently from Bitcoin itself.

Nevertheless, investment in financial infrastructure could support the industry’s long-term development by expanding payment services, custody capabilities, and access to digital assets.

ARK’s activity also arrives amid evidence of increasing interest from traditional financial institutions, including Wells Fargo’s reported Bitcoin ETF exposure.

Is Cathie Wood Positioning For A Crypto Recovery?

ARK’s latest transactions are noteworthy, but a single trading session cannot establish a lasting change in investment strategy.

The firm regularly adjusts portfolio allocations, and its daily trade disclosures do not establish whether proceeds from specific sales funded particular purchases.

What the numbers do demonstrate is that ARK was willing to increase selected crypto-related equity positions during a period of market weakness.

For Bitcoin investors, the development offers an interesting perspective on institutional positioning. Even when cryptocurrency prices experience significant volatility, investment firms may continue identifying opportunities in the businesses supporting digital asset adoption.

The next important signal will be whether ARK maintains or expands these positions in subsequent trading disclosures.

For now, the November 16 transactions suggest that Cathie Wood’s firm remains engaged with cryptocurrency infrastructure, even as it adjusts exposure across the broader technology sector.

The post Ransomware Gang Claims Visa and JPMorgan Chase as Victims, Sets 48-Hour Leak Deadline appeared first on The Daily Hodl.
fullContent:
A newly emerged ransomware gang has listed Visa and JPMorgan Chase as alleged victims and threatens to leak stolen data within 48 hours.

The gang, which goes by the name n0n, has given the two companies 48 hours to negotiate, reports Cybernews.

Visa says it is aware of the claims and that the incident involved a third-party service provider in the Asia Pacific region.

Says a Visa spokesperson,

“Visa’s systems were not involved and were not impacted. There is no indication that payment data such as card numbers have been affected.”

Visa has not said which third-party service providers were hit.

Meanwhile, JPMorgan Chase is separately dealing with a service outage that it blames on a software bug.

The bank says there is “no evidence” linking the disruption to a cyberattack.

The bank has not said whether the outage has any connection to the gang’s claims.

The n0n gang was first tracked in mid-September.

The gang claimed last week that it stole billions of traveler records from Expedia.

The attackers have offered few details about what they claim to have stolen from Visa and JPMorgan Chase.

The Daily HODL previously reported that JPMorgan Chase and other major US banks suffered a major outage that involved login failures and missing account balances.

title: XMR Gets a Clean Audit From zkSecurity as Monero Eyes 150M-Strong Anonymity Sets
description: Monero's bulletproofs code passed a zkSecurity audit with no serious flaws. XMR trades near $505, below its 50-day average, with the 200-day line as key support.
fullContent:
Three Things to Know

  • Monero's generalized bulletproofs code passed a zkSecurity audit with no high- or medium-severity findings.
  • XMR trades below its 50-day average while sellers still control momentum.
  • The 200-day average now serves as the line between a correction and a broken trend.

Monero's privacy upgrade cleared a key test this month. An outside review of the cryptography behind Full-Chain Membership Proofs found no serious flaws, and the team backed it with formal math proofs.

The market has shrugged so far. XMR kept sliding through the week, and sellers still set the pace. Traders want to know whether a stronger protocol can pull buyers back before the longer-term trend gives way.

zkSecurity Finds No Serious Flaws in Monero's Generalized Bulletproofs

Security firm zkSecurity found no high- or medium-severity flaws in Monero's generalized bulletproofs code. The firm reviewed the generalized-bulletproofs crate in monero-oxide, the project's Rust cryptography library, over ten working days. It flagged 4 low-severity issues and 3 informational items. Monero-oxide developers answered all seven.

MAGIC Grants, which contracted zkSecurity in June, announced the result on Nov. 12. Monero confirmed it on Nov. 18. Researchers Mathias Hall-Andersen and Suneal Gong led the review.

The work went beyond a standard code check. The team wrote a new proof of knowledge soundness and formalized the protocol in the Lean theorem prover. That process verified completeness, zero-knowledge and soundness, and the proofs sit publicly on GitHub.

This clears a major hurdle for FCMP++, or Full-Chain Membership Proofs. The upgrade would replace ring signatures and could widen anonymity sets to about 150 million outputs.

Several steps remain. MAGIC Grants announced a Trail of Bits review in August. The Community Crowdfunding System set aside 500 XMR for an integration audit, and a developer requested 45 XMR in October for three months of work. A second beta stressnet has run since May 6, starting at block 2,997,100.

Good News Meets a Price Stuck Under Its 50-Day Line

Monero (XMR) daily price with the nearest support (green) and resistance (red). Source: TradingView

Monero traded near $505 on Tuesday, little changed over the past 24 hours. The audit news landed during a slide, and the price has yet to respond to it.

XMR lost about 10% over the past seven days. Over 30 days the drop is closer to 16%. A clean security review lowers long-term risk for the network, but traders have kept selling anyway.

The moving averages show where the coin stands. A moving average smooths daily prices into one line, and traders use it to judge the trend. XMR now sits below its 50-day average near $557. That line tracks the medium-term trend, and the price falling under it means recent buyers are mostly sitting on losses. The 50-day level now acts as a ceiling that sellers can lean on.

Over a longer horizon, XMR looks healthier. XMR still holds above its 200-day average, around $474. That average measures the trend over most of a year, so the broader uptrend remains intact for now. The coin is caught between a weakening medium trend and a long trend that has not broken.

Tuesday's quiet session matters too. A flat day after a weekly loss suggests sellers are taking a break. It does not show buyers taking control. A real turn would need XMR to climb back toward the 50-day line.

Sellers Still Steer the Momentum

Momentum gauges tell the same story as the averages. RSI, a 0 to 100 gauge of momentum, sits at 38 on the daily chart. That reading is weak. It still sits above the oversold zone below 30, where selling often runs out of steam. XMR has room to slide further before buyers would see it as stretched.

The MACD adds to that view. It remains below its signal line, which means momentum is still pointing down. A separate trend-strength reading confirms a real trend, and sellers are the ones driving it.

Together, these signals set a high bar for any recovery. Traders would want to see momentum turn up and hold for several sessions before calling a bottom. Until then, short rallies look more like pauses inside a downtrend.

Why $535 Matters More Than the Distant Floor

Resistance sits close by, near $535. That level caps the first leg of any bounce. A daily close above it would put the 50-day line back in play as the next test. Clearing both would mark the first real sign that buyers are returning.

The support picture looks very different. The nearest listed floors sit far below the market, around $169 and then $145. Levels that distant offer little guidance for traders watching daily moves.

That leaves the 200-day average as the working cushion. It has held so far. A decisive drop through it would remove the last nearby support. That would open space toward the much lower floors.

Two Paths for the Next Three Days

Two setups stand out, and each hinges on a level already flagged above.

  • Bullish: A daily close above that nearby resistance would open the way toward the 50-day line. Momentum would need to turn up to support the move. The setup fails if XMR slips back under Tuesday's trading price.
  • Bearish: A clean break below the 200-day average would signal deeper losses, with little support close underneath. This view fails if buyers push XMR back above that nearby resistance.

A Stronger Protocol Still Waiting for Buyers

The audit gives Monero's privacy roadmap a stronger footing. Formal proofs and zero serious findings make FCMP++ look more credible to long-term holders. The price still argues for patience until XMR clears resistance.

Risks remain on both fronts. Further audits stand between the code and a release date, so FCMP++ timing is still open.

title: Singapore Opens Agentic Money Sandbox for AI Digital Payments
description:
The Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) and the Future of Finance Institute (FFI) outlined an Agentic Money Sandbox on November 18, 2026, at the Singapore FinTech Festival. The testbed lets banks try AI agents that start digital-money payments and treasury moves. Agents must stay inside set authority, limits, and safeguards before any live rollout. The […]
The post Singapore Opens Agentic Money Sandbox for AI Digital Payments appeared first on Live Bitcoin News.
fullContent:
The Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) and the Future of Finance Institute (FFI) outlined an Agentic Money Sandbox on November 18, 2026, at the Singapore FinTech Festival. The testbed lets banks try AI agents that start digital-money payments and treasury moves. Agents must stay inside set authority, limits, and safeguards before any live rollout.

The joint MAS and FFI release ties the sandbox to Singapore’s National AI Missions for financial services. Deputy Prime Minister Gan Kim Yong, who chairs MAS, named the third mission as enabling safe agentic transactions. In his SFF 2026 keynote, he said greater autonomy for agents must come with clear responsibility. Agents work inside set authority and limits. Institutions and enterprises stay accountable for actions taken on their behalf.

What the Agentic Money Sandbox Is Testing

FFI will run the sandbox as a shared lab, not a public retail product. Banks can build and exercise the controls AI agents need to move digital money safely. The release names early use cases as agent-initiated payments and treasury management across participating banks.

The stake is practical. An AI agent can pay a supplier, sweep idle cash, or settle an invoice without a human click on every step. That only helps if the bank can prove who authorized the agent, what it could spend, and who owns the loss if it misfires. The sandbox is where those proofs get stress-tested before live books take the hit.

MAS and FFI also named FFI’s bank launch partners at SFF 2026: DBS, OCBC, Standard Chartered, and UOB. Those banks sit with technology and research partners on the broader National AI Missions programme, not only on the money sandbox.

How Purpose-Bound Limits Are Meant to Constrain Agents

Gan’s keynote put one concrete control path on the table: purpose bound money. In that framing, conditions ride with the funds. An agent can move money only when preset rules are met. His examples are blunt. An agent could pay a contract once the terms have been checked. Or it could finish a purchase for a user inside limits already written into the money.

That is the mechanism in plain order. First the money carries a purpose, a cap, and a permission set. Then the agent checks whether those conditions hold. Then the payment fires. The trials must also examine identity, authority, accountability, and interoperability before wider use.

For AI and blockchain readers, the interesting split is not “AI decides” versus “a human clicks.” It is whether programmable limits on digital money can make an autonomous payment look more like a constrained instruction than an open wallet. Purpose-bound rails are the candidate answer MAS is willing to test. They are not a claim that every Singapore bank deposit is already programmable that way.

Why a Sandbox Matters Before Live Agentic Payments

Agent-led payments change the failure mode. A mistaken human transfer is usually one bad click. A mistaken agent can repeat a bad rule at machine speed across banks. Gan’s speech frames the upside as faster cash management and machine-led commerce. The same speech refuses to detach that upside from accountability under financial regulation.

The sandbox therefore has a dual job. It asks what value agents can create in payments and treasury. It also asks which safeguards must exist before those agents leave the lab. Banks need shared ways to prove identity, grant authority, assign accountability, and work across institutions.

Xinhua independently reported the same Wednesday package. FFI is establishing the Agentic Money Sandbox so banks can test AI agents that conduct digital-money transactions inside defined limits and safeguards. The wire matches the MAS fact pattern. It does not add a go-live date or production volumes.

What Is Demonstrated, and Where the Catch Sits

What the primary record shows today is a named testbed and a policy frame. MAS and FFI announced the Agentic Money Sandbox. Initial cases are agent payments and treasury management. Purpose bound money is an explicit trial area in the chairman’s keynote. Four large banks are listed as FFI launch partners. The sandbox’s stated job is to test controls before live deployment.

What remains unproven is harder and more important. The release does not publish a start date for live agent traffic. It also skips a schedule of which payment rails will sit under the sandbox, and it shows no results from completed agent payment drills. Embedding conditions into money can constrain an agent’s spending. It does not prove the agent’s judgment about a contract, an invoice, or a treasury move was correct. Verification of permission is not verification of good decisions.

The mental model to keep is simple. Singapore is not declaring that AI agents already run the country’s digital payments. It is building a controlled room where banks practice letting agents move digital money under purpose-bound limits, identity checks, and clear accountability. Only then will they decide what is safe to take live.

title: DHS chief defends football trip as Congress presses him over nationwide ground stop
description:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, in testimony Wednesday to Congress, defended his flight to a weekend college football game, tried to tamp down speculation about a series of recent cyber outages and found himself pressed repeatedly on training given to the country's immigration enforcement officers.
The hearing before the House Homeland Security Committee, a standard yearly opportunity for lawmakers to question administration officials about national security threats, covered a broad range of topics. It also gave Democrats, after their recent midterm drubbing of Republicans, a chance to confront a Cabinet member.
A look at some of the highlights:
Officials keep trying to reassure Americans over computer system disruptions 
Mullin and the two other witnesses, FBI Deputy Director Christopher Raia and Jay Clayton, the director of national intelligence, insisted that the high-profile outages across the government and private sector over the past week had no connection to each other and did not result from a cyberattack or nefarious activity.
“I understand the timing of these incidents can raise questions, and it should. The American people should ask us these questions," Clayton said. “But based on what we know today,” he said, "these are separate service outages associated with maintenance and technical changes. They are not a coordinated or state sponsored attack.”
Among the events were an hourslong outage in Microsoft services; a nationwide ground stop brought about by a technology upgrade on the nation’s air traffic control system that overloaded antiquated equipment and caused “intermittent” communications and radar gaps; banking problems that rippled through the financial industry; and a disruption to a classified internal communications network at the National Security Agency.
The episodes stirred widespread public concern that they could be linked or caused by hackers. Officials said there was no evidence of that.
“I'm 98% confident that this has nothing to do with our adversaries hacking or going after our systems,” Mullin said.
Those statements of reassurance came against the backdrop of concerns about the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, which is part of Mullin's Department of Homeland Security. It is tasked with working with industry to protect infrastructure, including water and electric generation, election systems, chemical facilities and cyber networks.
That agency has been without a Senate-confirmed leader since President Donald Trump took office for a second term in early 2025. Trump’s original pick withdrew his nomination earlier this year after it had languished for months in the Senate. The agency also lost staff last year during cuts aimed at reducing the size of the government.
Mullin flew to a football game as travelers were scrambling
Mullin defended his decision to fly to Louisiana on Saturday for the LSU-Texas game as travelers across the United States were still stuck at airports after the nationwide grounding of flights. 
Mullin’s flight took place after the stoppage was lifted and as planes were back in the air. But thousands of flights were canceled because of the ground stop, and Mullin flew as people nationwide were forced to scramble for alternative travel options.
On Wednesday, he said canceling the trip could have sent a confusing message.
Mullin said his travel had been planned for weeks so he could take relatives to the game and there was discussion before the trip about whether to forgo it.
“If we canceled something with the airspace completely open, it could bring confusion because I was meeting the governor there. I was meeting other people there that would show maybe distrust that we’re not even willing to fly,” Mullin said.
Mullin reiterated that he is required to fly on government planes and that he paid for the trip.
Mullin defends ground stop response
Mullin was front and center in the Republican administration's response to the grounding of all aircraft last week.
The administration has said the ground stop was the result of problems with newly installed routers that caused the Federal Aviation Administration’s telecommunications system to be flooded with data, forcing the agency to ground all flights while it addressed the issue.
At the hearing, Mullin pushed back on criticism that the administration wasn't giving the public clear answers.
“We were able to put the planes back in the air safely. We landed over 4,000 planes when the ground stoppage went out because of the communication and didn’t have one single incident. That in itself is a great success," Mullin said.
Immigration enforcement under new scrutiny
Lawmakers focused part of their scrutiny of Mullin on immigration enforcement actions that have led to fatal encounters with federal officers. Also discussed was shortened training and the vetting of some newly hired agents.
U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement has had an unprecedented hiring surge, bringing on 12,000 new officers and special agents. The employment rush has raised questions about whether the government lowered standards and conducted incomplete background checks. In one prominent case, an ICE officer with what his family and records say was a history of violent behavior shot and killed a Colombian man in Maine.
Mullin said every ICE officer in service now has had a full background check and that those who have not are on administrative leave. Officers who have not completed a full 13 weeks of training also have been placed on leave until they conclude their training, he said.
The deaths of U.S. citizens such as Renee Good and Alex Pretti in Minneapolis led to a tense exchange when Rep. LaMonica McIver, D-N.J., asked Mullin if he had any regrets over his role in enforcing Trump’s immigration agenda. 
Mullin said he had none. Then McIver pressed him about apologies for the deaths. 
“You are killing people,” McIver replied. 
“No ma’am. That’s your opinion,” Mullin said, ending the exchange.
Mullin took over DHS after Kristi Noem was ousted in March when the deaths of the Minnesota protesters at the hands of immigration enforcement officers forced the administration to adjust its mass deportation strategy. 
Immigration arrests initially fell but then rebounded as ICE, flush with billions of dollars in new congressional funding, hired new officers and maximized cooperation from local and state law enforcement agencies.
Trump has indicated after the Nov. 3 election losses that he could work with Democrats on immigration legislation, but he has also elevated Stephen Miller, the architect of his immigration crackdown, to be his chief of staff.
___
Associated Press writers Josh Funk in Omaha, Nebraska, and Valerie Gonzalez in McAllen, Texas, contributed to this report.
This article originally appeared on Associated Press at https://www.yahoo.com/news/articles/mullin-heads-congress-questions-swirl-120158124.html

title: Standard Chartered Sees LINK at $200 by 2030, but Chainlink First Has to Hold $7
description: Standard Chartered sees Chainlink's LINK at $200 by 2030 on tokenized asset growth. The chart still favors sellers, with support near $7.83 and $7 in focus.
fullContent:
Three Things to Know

  • Standard Chartered says LINK could reach $200 by 2030 on the back of tokenized asset growth.
  • The chart still favors sellers, with LINK stuck below both of its key moving averages.
  • Traders are watching whether the token can hold the $7 area if nearer support gives way.

Standard Chartered has set a long-range target for Chainlink's LINK, betting that tokenized assets will drive demand for its cross-chain services. The call lands while the token sits deep in a monthlong slide.

Bank pilots keep coming, yet they have not turned into fees for token holders. Spot ETF investors have started pulling money, too. Traders now face a simple question: can buyers defend the lows long enough for adoption to catch up?

A $200 Call Arrives as Partnerships Stay on Testnet

Standard Chartered expects Chainlink's LINK token to reach $200 by the end of 2030. That would mean a gain of nearly 22x from today's level. The bank ties the call to tokenized assets growing to $4 trillion by the end of 2028. Chainlink sells the plumbing that moves data and value between blockchains, so more tokenized assets could mean more demand for its services.

Big names are already testing that plumbing. Moody's launched a credit-data pilot on Nov 10 that uses Chainlink's CCIP to send ratings across networks, though it runs on testnet only. Korean broker Hanwha Investment & Securities integrated CCIP for its tokenization platform on Oct 29. None of this generates fees for the token yet.

ETF investors have grown impatient. Cumulative net inflows into the spot funds GLNK and CLNK slipped to $174.4 million by Nov 16. That followed four straight days of outflows. Total net assets fell about 30%, to $157.5 million. LINK now sits 82.7% below its $52.70 record.

Both Key Averages Now Sit Overhead

Chainlink (LINK) daily price with the nearest support (green) and resistance (red). Source: TradingView

LINK traded near $9.14 on Tuesday, down about 2% over the past day. The token has lost roughly 24% in a month. That slide leaves the chart in a weak spot.

The drop has been steady. LINK changed hands near $12 on Oct 21. It fell below $9 by mid-November. That move set the range traders now watch, with the October high as the ceiling and the mid-November lows as the floor.

A moving average smooths out daily prices over a set number of days, so it shows the general direction. The 50-day average tracks the recent trend and sits near $11.08. The 200-day average tracks the longer trend and sits near $10.88.

LINK trades below both lines. Analysts read that as a bearish setup, because each average now acts as a ceiling that sellers can defend. Rallies toward those levels tend to meet supply from holders looking to exit near their entry price.

The 50-day average also sits above the 200-day. That gap shows how fast the recent selling erased gains from earlier months.

A daily close back above the 200-day line would be the first sign of repair. That would tell traders that buyers have taken back the longer trend. Until then, any bounce looks like a pause inside a downtrend.

Sellers Still Hold the Momentum Edge

Momentum readings back up what the averages show. RSI, a 0 to 100 gauge of momentum, sits near 33. That reading is weak, though it has not yet reached the oversold zone below 30. In plain terms, sellers still have room to push before the market looks stretched.

LINK dropped about 11% over the past week, and buyers have not stepped in with any force.

MACD, a tool that compares short and longer price trends, stays below its signal line. That means momentum is still pointing down. Trend strength readings also confirm a real trend, and sellers are the ones leading it.

$7.83 Is the Last Floor Before $7

Support sits near $7.83, with no mapped level below it. A clean break there would leave the $7 area from the headline as the next real test. Losing that area would push the bank's target further out of reach.

Buyers have a shorter list of hurdles on the upside. The first resistance sits near $10.27, where recent bounces have stalled. Above that, the next ceiling stands near $10.91, almost on top of the 200-day line.

A rally would have to clear two sell zones packed close together. Until LINK closes above both, sellers keep control of the range between these levels.

Where the Next Three Days Could Lead

Two paths stand out for the coming sessions, and each depends on one level breaking first.

  • Bullish: A daily close above first resistance would open the way to the next ceiling, the one sitting almost on the 200-day line. That would hint that buyers are starting to absorb supply. The setup fails if LINK slips below its current support.
  • Bearish: Losing that support would put the headline floor in play as the next target. Sellers would then be pressing toward lows not seen in this slide. A move back above first resistance would cancel this view.

Adoption Needs a Floor to Stand On

The bank's tokenization thesis still holds on paper, and the pilots show real interest. The chart tells a harder story. Sellers keep the edge until LINK reclaims the nearest resistance and the 200-day line.

Spot funds remain the main risk. Another run of ETF outflows could add supply and speed a break of support.

title: Michael Saylor Says Banks Are Bringing Bitcoin To Clients — But Who Really Owns The $2.35 Billion?
description: Michael Saylor has drawn attention to a remarkable shift in Wall Street’s relationship with Bitcoin, highlighting how Wells Fargo’s brokerage businesses more than doubled their holdings of BlackRock’s Bitcoin exchange-traded fund during the third quarter. But behind the impressive numbers lies an even more interesting question: who is actually accumulating Bitcoin exposure? The comments arrive […]
fullContent:
Michael Saylor has drawn attention to a remarkable shift in Wall Street’s relationship with Bitcoin, highlighting how Wells Fargo’s brokerage businesses more than doubled their holdings of BlackRock’s Bitcoin exchange-traded fund during the third quarter. But behind the impressive numbers lies an even more interesting question: who is actually accumulating Bitcoin exposure?

The comments arrive shortly after Bitcoinist reported that Wells Fargo and its associated investment businesses disclosed approximately $2.35 billion in BlackRock’s iShares Bitcoin Trust (IBIT) shares.

While the headline figure suggests substantial institutional participation, the underlying regulatory filing reveals a more nuanced development that could be particularly important for Bitcoin’s long-term adoption.

Rather than representing a single corporate investment, much of the reported exposure is associated with brokerage and wealth-management operations.

Michael Saylor Highlights A Major Shift In Bitcoin Ownership

Strategy Executive Chairman Michael Saylor recently took to X to highlight the growing role of traditional banks in connecting customers with Bitcoin.

Saylor pointed out that two Wells Fargo brokerage businesses reported approximately 42 million shares of BlackRock’s Bitcoin ETF at the end of September, compared with roughly 20 million shares at the end of June.

The increase represents approximately 110% growth in reported shares over three months.

The figures are particularly interesting because the two brokerage businesses account for the majority of Wells Fargo’s overall IBIT position.

According to the company’s official SEC filing, Wells Fargo and its associated investment managers reported 49,577,094 IBIT shares as of September 30.

That compares with 24,396,222 shares at the end of June, representing an increase of approximately 103%.

However, these figures should not be interpreted as Wells Fargo purchasing $2.35 billion in Bitcoin for its own corporate treasury.

The filing includes positions associated with different investment-management entities, including securities managed or held for clients.

This distinction could be even more significant than the headline number itself.

Why Brokerage Clients Could Become Important For Bitcoin

For years, institutional Bitcoin adoption was closely associated with corporate treasury purchases and investment funds.

Companies such as Strategy helped establish Bitcoin as an asset that corporations could hold on their balance sheets.

However, the expansion of regulated Bitcoin ETFs has created another route for investors to access the cryptocurrency.

Instead of purchasing Bitcoin through specialized exchanges, investors can obtain exposure through conventional brokerage accounts, financial advisers, and wealth-management platforms.

Wells Fargo’s latest filing provides an example of how substantial this distribution channel has become.

Its two largest brokerage-related IBIT positions accounted for approximately 84.7% of the group’s reported shares.

This suggests that the growth of Bitcoin exposure through traditional financial services deserves closer attention.

Nevertheless, the filing does not identify every underlying investor or establish how much of the reported increase came from new retail customers rather than existing institutional accounts.

What it does demonstrate is that Bitcoin-linked securities are becoming an increasingly established part of conventional investment infrastructure.

The $2.35 Billion Figure Tells Only Part Of The Story

Another important consideration is the difference between the number of ETF shares held and their reported market value.

Wells Fargo’s aggregate IBIT share count increased approximately 103% between June and September.

However, the reported value of those shares increased from approximately $812 million to $2.35 billion, a gain of roughly 189%.

The difference reflects both the higher share count and changes in IBIT’s market valuation.

This distinction matters because a rising reported position value does not necessarily represent an equivalent amount of new capital entering Bitcoin.

Furthermore, the September 30 filing represents a historical snapshot.

It cannot establish whether Wells Fargo’s associated accounts maintained, reduced, or expanded their exposure during Bitcoin’s more recent market correction.

As Bitcoinist previously highlighted, BlackRock’s IBIT experienced a period of withdrawals before attracting renewed inflows on November 16.

The contrast between earlier quarterly accumulation and more recent ETF volatility demonstrates why institutional adoption should be evaluated over longer periods rather than through individual trading sessions.

Could Wall Street Distribution Become Bitcoin’s Next Major Growth Driver?

Saylor’s comments arrive as Bitcoin continues navigating a challenging market environment.

Although price volatility has affected investor sentiment, the expansion of traditional investment channels remains an important structural development.

Banks and brokerage platforms already maintain relationships with millions of customers, providing infrastructure that could make Bitcoin exposure more accessible to investors who prefer familiar financial products.

This does not mean every brokerage customer will purchase Bitcoin, nor does it guarantee that ETF demand will consistently increase.

Indeed, recent Bitcoin ETF withdrawals demonstrate that investors can reduce exposure just as quickly as they increase it.

However, the growing availability of regulated Bitcoin products represents a meaningful difference from earlier cryptocurrency market cycles.

Bitcoin no longer depends exclusively on specialized trading platforms to reach potential investors.

What Happens Next For Bitcoin Institutional Adoption?

We believe the most important takeaway from Saylor’s comments is not simply that Wells Fargo reported billions of dollars in Bitcoin ETF exposure.

It is that traditional brokerage infrastructure has become an important channel through which investors can participate in the Bitcoin market.

The next quarterly disclosures will help determine whether the growth reported in September continued during the subsequent period of market volatility.

For now, the latest figures reinforce a constructive long-term trend: Bitcoin is becoming increasingly accessible through established financial institutions.

And while short-term price movements remain uncertain, the expansion of traditional distribution channels could become one of the most important developments shaping Bitcoin adoption over the coming years.

title: Coinbase Brings ChatGPT Into Crypto Trading as Pancake Rebrand Signals Binance Rivalry
description:
Coinbase brings crypto trading to ChatGPT as Pancake drops Swap from its name, raising the stakes in the race against Binance DeFi ecosystem.
The post Coinbase Brings ChatGPT Into Crypto Trading as Pancake Rebrand Signals Binance Rivalry appeared first on Cryptonews.
fullContent:
Coinbase is bringing crypto trading directly into ChatGPT as competition for AI-powered financial services intensifies. Meanwhile, PancakeSwap has dropped “Swap” from its name, expanding beyond decentralized trading. The two developments show how Coinbase and Binance-linked crypto projects are positioning themselves for the next phase of digital finance.

Coinbase announced its ChatGPT integration last night, allowing users to connect accounts and manage portfolios. Users can check balances, analyze holdings, and place eligible trades using everyday language. And every order requires explicit approval before execution.

The timing coincides with Pancake’s attempt to reposition itself beyond its original decentralized exchange business.

Discover: The Best Token Presales

Coinbase Brings Crypto Trading Directly Into ChatGPT

The Coinbase plugin allows eligible users to trade crypto and equities without leaving ChatGPT. Users can request market or limit orders through conversational instructions.

Before execution, ChatGPT displays an interactive confirmation card showing order details. Users must approve the transaction before Coinbase processes it through its Advanced Trade platform. Standard trading fees, eligibility requirements, and account limits still apply.

Coinbase CEO Brian Armstrong described the integration as another step toward an emerging agentic economy. The idea involves AI assistants handling increasingly complex financial tasks for users. But Coinbase still keeps humans responsible for approving individual trades for now.

The integration also builds on Coinbase’s AI infrastructure. Its Coinbase for Agents toolkit provides developers with connections to trading accounts and market data. The ChatGPT launch brings those capabilities into a more accessible consumer interface.

As of today, the official integration currently remains limited to eligible U.S. Coinbase users. It also depends on ChatGPT account and workspace availability.

Pancake Rebrand Takes Binance’s DeFi Ecosystem Beyond Swaps

While Coinbase expands through ChatGPT, Pancake is changing how users perceive its decentralized trading ecosystem. Formerly known as PancakeSwap, the platform announced its rebrand today. The new identity reflects six years of expansion beyond its original token-swapping business.

Pancake now operates across more than 11 blockchain networks. The platform reports over 208 million users and more than $4.4 trillion in cumulative trading volume.

Pancakeswap (CAKE)
24h7d30d1yAll time

Its services now include perpetual contracts, tokenized stocks, ETFs, yield products, and developer infrastructure. The project is also preparing a dedicated mobile application. Its CAKE ticker and contract address remain unchanged, with existing staking positions unaffected.

Pancake’s relationship with Binance makes this rebrand interesting. Binance Labs announced a strategic investment in CAKE in June 2022. The investment supported the decentralized exchange’s development within the BNB Chain ecosystem.

Coinbase and Binance Compete for the Future of AI Trading

The rivalry becomes clearer when looking beyond the latest announcements. Binance has already introduced its own AI infrastructure through Binance Agent OS. Launched in August 2026, the platform connects compatible AI applications with Binance trading, market data, wallet, and payment capabilities.

Its Model Context Protocol server supports compatible AI agents, including ChatGPT. Developers can build applications that access supported Binance services through user-controlled permissions.

Pancake is also developing its position in this emerging market. In July, the platform partnered with BNB Chain’s Agent Studio to help developers deploy autonomous agents.

These agents can interact with Pancake’s liquidity pools, rebalance positions, and execute trading strategies. Its AI tools also include portfolio planning and assistance across DeFi products.

This creates an interesting contrast between the two ecosystems. Coinbase is bringing AI-powered trading directly to consumers through ChatGPT. Binance is building infrastructure that allows developers and AI agents to interact with its services. Pancake adds a decentralized execution layer to the wider BNB Chain ecosystem.

The next battle in crypto may not be about which exchange attracts the most human traders. It could be about which infrastructure becomes the preferred destination for AI-powered financial activity.

title: Why a 5% Stablecoin Return Can Still Cost Holders Money
description:
Key TakeAways A steady peg doesn’t protect euro value. A 10% euro rise cancels 10% yield. Two conversion fees push […]
The post Why a 5% Stablecoin Return Can Still Cost Holders Money appeared first on Coindoo.
fullContent:
Key TakeAways

  • A steady peg doesn’t protect euro value.
  • A 10% euro rise cancels 10% yield.
  • Two conversion fees push the hurdle higher.
  • EU rules ban interest on e-money tokens.

In September 2026, the European Banking Authority urged the Commission to consider regulating crypto-asset lending, the kind of business that sits behind stablecoin yields offered to Europeans.

For anyone who swapped euros to earn one, that yield has a catch. Our earlier piece showed why a perfect dollar peg can still cost holders euros. This one works out how much return it takes to cover that gap, where a return can legally come from in the EU, and what the extra dollar yield is really paying for.

A 5% return that ends €455 short

Start with €10,000 and an exchange rate of 1.10, so one euro buys $1.10. Ignore fees for now. The saver receives 11,000 tokens, each redeemable for $1.

A lending product then adds 5% over twelve months, lifting the balance to 11,550 tokens. The peg never slips.

The euro moves instead. By year-end EUR/USD sits at 1.21, and those 11,550 tokens convert back to €9,545.45. That leaves the saver €454.55 down after a year of positive returns.

The currency side of this is the trap our earlier piece walked through: a 10% euro rise cuts a dollar balance’s euro value by about 9.09%. What changes here is the yield. With no return, the saver would have ended at €9,090.91. The 5% claws back half of that damage. Half.

The return you need just to get your euros back

With the peg intact and no costs, one line covers it:

Required return = exit rate ÷ entry rate – 1

Here that’s 1.21 ÷ 1.10 – 1, or 10%. Earn less and the saver loses money in euro terms, however good the dollar figure looks.

Fees lift the bar. Assume 0.5% goes on the way in and another 0.5% on the way out, round numbers chosen for illustration rather than taken from any provider’s price list. Only €9,950 gets converted, buying 10,945 tokens, and the exit fee trims whatever comes back. Both deductions enter the formula:

Required return = (exit rate ÷ entry rate) ÷ (0.995 × 0.995) – 1

At 1.21, the hurdle rises to about 11.11%. The same 5% year now returns €9,450.24. Swap in your own platform’s fees and the formula still works.

Euro weakens to 1.00

No yield, no fees: €11,000.00

5% yield, no fees: €11,550.00

5% yield, with fees: €11,434.79

Yield needed after fees: none

Rate stays at 1.10

No yield, no fees: €10,000.00

5% yield, no fees: €10,500.00

5% yield, with fees: €10,395.26

Yield needed after fees: about 1.01%

Euro strengthens to 1.21

No yield, no fees: €9,090.91

5% yield, no fees: €9,545.45

5% yield, with fees: €9,450.24

Yield needed after fees: about 11.11%

Hypothetical scenarios calculated by the Coindoo team for €10,000 converted at 1.10 and held for one year. Tokens stay at $1, fees are 0.5% per conversion, and the figures exclude taxes and inflation.

A weaker euro gives the saver a currency gain with no yield at all. A flat rate makes fees the main obstacle, small but real. A stronger euro is the case that hurts, and it turns a respectable 5% into a loss.

Real routes rarely cost a neat 0.5%. Trading fees, exchange spreads, network charges and bank fees stack up, and fixed charges bite harder on small balances. Redemption has its own catch. Under Circle’s EEA redemption policy, retail USDC holders need an account that can receive dollars, and Circle warns that banks may charge for incoming payments or currency conversion. A $1 redemption claim tells you very little about the euros that finally land in your account.

Breaking even also has a narrow meaning here: the same number of euros back. It ignores inflation. And it skips the obvious question of what those euros could have earned without ever leaving the currency.

What the extra dollar yield pays for

Dollar returns tend to sit above euro returns because US policy rates do. The Federal Reserve held its target range at 3.75% to 4% on October 28. A day later, the ECB kept its deposit rate at 2.50%.

That gap of roughly 1.25 to 1.5 percentage points isn’t free money. A saver who wanted the dollar return without the currency exposure would have to hedge it, and in currency markets the cost of hedging tracks the interest-rate difference between the two currencies. Economists call this covered interest parity. In plain terms: remove the currency risk and most of the extra yield goes with it.

Skip the hedge and the saver keeps the premium, along with the risk the cards above show. Part of any dollar stablecoin yield above euro rates is payment for carrying that risk, whatever the platform calls it.

Crypto lending rates don’t move one-for-one with central banks. Borrower demand sets them, and they can swing far from policy rates. The currency trade-off stays the same either way.

READ MORE:

The World Bank’s USDC Plan Has a Problem Nobody Mentions

In the EU, the issuer can’t pay you that 5%

So where does a European’s stablecoin return come from? Not from the token. Circle’s EU white paper for USDC describes a token backed by dollar-denominated assets and redeemable 1:1 for dollars. Holding it earns nothing.

MiCA Article 50 closes the obvious shortcut. It bars e-money-token issuers and crypto-asset service providers from granting interest on those tokens, and it counts any reward linked to how long you hold them as interest, whatever the label. A regulated EU exchange can’t pay you for simply keeping USDC in your account.

Any advertised yield therefore points somewhere else: a lending arrangement, a DeFi protocol, or a platform operating outside that rule. Every one of them puts your tokens in someone else’s hands. Ask who borrows them, what secures the loan, whether withdrawals can be paused, and whether the rate is fixed or resets daily. The 5% in our example is a completed year’s return, while an advertised annual rate can change long before the year is out.

That lending business, including activity linked to DeFi, is exactly what the EBA wants brought under rules. MiCA doesn’t cover it today.

When dollars fit, and when EURC makes more sense

None of this makes a dollar balance a mistake. If you have a dollar invoice to pay or dollar income coming in, you already hold the right currency, and the euro rate barely touches you.

Euro spenders face a different test. Circle describes EURC as redeemable 1:1 for euros, which takes the currency mismatch off the table. Switching currency leaves issuer, custody and platform risk where they were. What it removes is the exchange-rate line from the calculation.

Before converting, write down three numbers: the rate you get in at, the total cost of the round trip, and the return the product has actually paid in the past rather than the one on the banner. The yield left after fees is the size of euro rally the balance can absorb. A bigger rally eats the gain, however many tokens you’ve added.
